title: A Momentum-Regulated Model For Star Formation Efficiency in Giant Molecular Clouds
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (16 pages, 5 figures)
summary: We present a minimal analytic framework to investigate the star formation efficiency per free-fall time, $ε_{\rm ff}$, in giant molecular clouds (GMCs), focusing on the origin of the observed clustering around $ε_{\rm ff} \sim 0.01$. We model the time evolution of the turbulent velocity dispersion through a momentum balance between stellar feedback and turbulent dissipation, and show that this generically leads to a stable low-efficiency equilibrium with only weak dependence on global cloud properties. We extend the framework by including a phenomenological contribution from gravity-driven turbulence and find that both feedback- and gravity-driven motions converge to similar equilibrium states under typical GMC conditions. The efficiency can be expressed as the ratio between a gravitational velocity scale and an effective feedback velocity scale, providing a physically transparent interpretation of self-regulated star formation. The model provides a simple, physically motivated interpretation of observed gas-star formation scaling relations, including a Schmidt-like scaling at cloud scales and a Kennicutt-like scaling when averaged over cloud populations. Comparison with observed GMC properties shows agreement within a factor of a few and highlights the weak sensitivity of $ε_{\rm ff}$ to cloud parameters. Despite its simplicity, the framework captures the leading-order interplay between turbulence, gravity, and feedback, and provides a physically transparent explanation for the origin and robustness of low star formation efficiencies in GMCs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a minimal analytic model showing that star formation efficiency per free-fall time (ε_ff) in GMCs clusters around ~0.01 due to a self-regulated equilibrium between turbulent dissipation and stellar feedback, with weak dependence on global cloud properties.
AI.motivation: To explain the observed clustering of ε_ff ≈ 0.01 in GMCs and understand why star formation efficiency is both low and relatively insensitive to global cloud conditions.
AI.method: A minimal analytic framework modeling the time evolution of turbulent velocity dispersion via momentum balance between stellar feedback and turbulent dissipation, extended with gravity-driven turbulence contributions.
AI.result: The efficiency can be expressed as the ratio between a gravitational velocity scale and an effective feedback velocity scale, yielding a stable low-efficiency equilibrium (ε_ff ∼ 0.01) with weak sensitivity to cloud parameters. The model reproduces Schmidt-like scaling at cloud scales and Kennicutt-like scaling over cloud populations, agreeing with observations within a factor of a few.
AI.conclusion: Despite its simplicity, the framework captures the leading-order interplay between turbulence, gravity, and feedback, providing a physically transparent explanation for the origin and robustness of low star formation efficiencies in GMCs.

title: Kinetic Processes to Radio Burst: First Observational-driven Study in Coronal Loops
summary: Understanding the origin of coherent solar radio bursts requires linking macroscopic coronal structures with the kinetic processes responsible for wave generation. We investigate emissions from slowly positively drifting bursts (SPDBs), a specific type of solar radio emission. SPDBs provide observational constraints for modeling beam-plasma interactions in coronal loops, serving as a basis for a multiscale description. We employ a three--stage numerical framework that combines nonlinear force--free field (NLFFF) magnetic extrapolation, guiding--center simulations, and fully kinetic particle--in--cell (PIC) modeling. The background plasma density is described using a hydrostatic model consistent with active--region conditions, producing a plasma--frequency gradient comparable to that inferred from the observed SPDBs spectrum. Energetic electrons injected near the loop top evolve through magnetic mirroring, pitch--angle scattering, turbulence development, and partial precipitation. Evolved velocity distribution functions (EVDFs) are sampled after approximately one bounce period and used in PIC simulations to evaluate emission properties. The results show that the evolved beam distribution of energetic electrons predominantly excites beam--Langmuir waves and fundamental plasma emission along the loop, with the emission intensity gradually decreasing from the loop top toward the footpoint. The modest initial beam velocity of energetic electrons explains the inefficient generation of harmonic plasma emission. The temporal evolution of the modeled emission reproduces key SPDB characteristics, including the ~ 4s duration and frequency drift behavior. These results suggest plasma emission explains the mechanisms behind SPDB generation and demonstrate the feasibility of a unified model connecting coronal magnetic topology, particle transport, and radio emission.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a three-stage numerical framework (NLFFF extrapolation, guiding-center simulations, and PIC modeling) to study slowly positively drifting bursts (SPDBs) in the solar corona. Energetic electrons injected near loop tops produce beam-Langmuir waves and fundamental plasma emission via beam-plasma interactions, with emission intensity decreasing from loop top to footpoint. The model reproduces key SPDB characteristics (~4s duration and frequency drift), demonstrating a unified multiscale model connecting coronal magnetic topology, particle transport, and radio emission.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of coherent solar radio bursts by linking macroscopic coronal structures with kinetic processes responsible for wave generation, using SPDBs as observational constraints for modeling beam-plasma interactions in coronal loops.
AI.method: A three-stage numerical framework: (1) nonlinear force-free field (NLFFF) magnetic extrapolation, (2) guiding-center simulations of energetic electron transport including magnetic mirroring and pitch-angle scattering, and (3) fully kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) modeling using evolved velocity distribution functions (EVDFs) sampled after one bounce period.
AI.result: Evolved beam distributions predominantly excite beam-Langmuir waves and fundamental plasma emission along the loop; emission intensity decreases from loop top to footpoint; modest initial beam velocity suppresses harmonic plasma emission; the model reproduces ~4s duration and frequency drift characteristics of SPDBs.
AI.conclusion: Plasma emission explains SPDB generation mechanisms. The unified model demonstrates feasibility of connecting coronal magnetic topology, particle transport, and radio emission in a multiscale description.

title: J-PLUS: Spectral classification and photometric redshifts for 79 million sources in the fourth data release
comment: 16 pages, 14 figures, 1 table, 3 appendices. Submitted to A&A
summary: We present spectral classifications and photometric redshifts for 79.2 million sources up to an r-band magnitude of 22 in Data Release 4 of the Javalambre Photometric Local Universe Survey (J-PLUS). Leveraging the 12-band J-PLUS filter system, we compare a template-fitting approach (LePhare) against LeMoNNADE, a morphology-blind machine learning pipeline that uses spectral mixing augmentation to overcome training set limitations. LeMoNNADE consistently outperforms template fitting in precision, robust scatter, and outlier rates. Including WISE infrared photometry breaks optical degeneracies between stars and quasars, reducing the catastrophic outlier rate for quasars from ~40% to ~23% and constraining systemic redshift bias to <1% up to z = 4. We find LeMoNNADE is also less susceptible to redshift aliasing, particularly when adopting the probability density function median. Because the spectroscopic training samples severely under-represent stars, we apply an Expectation-Maximization Bayesian calibration to recover unbiased class probabilities for the magnitude-limited sample. This reveals that extragalactic counts agree with the literature down to the r ~ 20.5 completeness limit. The inferred redshift distribution for r < 21 extragalactic sources peaks at z ~ 0.3, showing broad agreement with existing literature up to z ~ 0.6. The resulting catalogues represent a significant milestone for local Universe science, offering probabilistically calibrated classifications and distances while explicitly characterising faint-end limits and contamination.

AI.tldr: This paper presents spectral classifications and photometric redshifts for 79.2 million sources in J-PLUS DR4, using a machine learning pipeline (LeMoNNADE) that outperforms template fitting (LePhare), with WISE IR data reducing quasar outlier rates from ~40% to ~23%, and EM Bayesian calibration recovering unbiased class probabilities.
AI.motivation: To provide probabilistically calibrated classifications and photometric redshifts for millions of sources in J-PLUS DR4, overcoming limitations of spectroscopic training sets and template-fitting approaches, particularly for separating stars from quasars.
AI.method: Compared LePhare (template fitting) vs. LeMoNNADE (machine learning with spectral mixing augmentation) using 12-band J-PLUS photometry plus WISE IR data; applied Expectation-Maximization Bayesian calibration to correct for underrepresented stellar classes in spectroscopic training samples.
AI.result: LeMoNNADE outperformed LePhare in precision, scatter, and outlier rates; WISE IR data reduced quasar catastrophic outlier rate from ~40% to ~23% and constrained redshift bias <1% up to z=4; extragalactic counts agree with literature to r~20.5; redshift distribution peaks at z~0.3 for r<21 sources.
AI.conclusion: The resulting catalogues represent a significant milestone for local Universe science, offering probabilistically calibrated classifications and distances with explicit characterization of faint-end limits and contamination.

title: A redshift of z=3.20 for the bright arc in eMACSJ2229.9-0808: Comment on Wagner & Falco (2026) "Hamilton's Object revisited: A challenging source redshift of a strong lensing configuration"
comment: Comment article in A&A, in press. Refers to arXiv:2604.19867
summary: We re-analyse near-infrared and optical spectroscopy from the Subaru, Gemini, and Keck telescopes of the bright gravitational arc seen in the z=0.62 X-ray cluster eMACSJ2229.9-0808. The 22 strongest spectral features we identify uniquely determine the redshift of the galaxy as z=3.20, as previously reported by Ebeling et al. (2025), not z=0.82 as claimed by Wagner & Falco (2026).

AI.tldr: Re-analysis of NIR/optical spectroscopy of a gravitational arc in cluster eMACSJ2229.9-0808 confirms the galaxy's redshift is z=3.20 (consistent with Ebeling et al. 2025), not z=0.82 as claimed by Wagner & Falco (2026), based on 22 identified spectral features.
AI.motivation: To resolve a discrepancy in the reported redshift of a bright gravitational arc in the X-ray cluster eMACSJ2229.9-0808, where two different values (z=3.20 vs. z=0.82) have been claimed.
AI.method: Re-analysis of near-infrared and optical spectroscopy from Subaru, Gemini, and Keck telescopes, identifying the 22 strongest spectral features to determine the galaxy's redshift.
AI.result: The 22 spectral features uniquely determine the redshift as z=3.20, consistent with Ebeling et al. (2025) and rejecting the z=0.82 claim by Wagner & Falco (2026).
AI.conclusion: The correct redshift of the gravitational arc galaxy is z=3.20, supporting the earlier finding by Ebeling et al. (2025) over the alternative claim.

title: CRexit observed: probing cosmic ray transport in the circumgalactic medium with absorption line spectra
summary: Cosmic rays (CRs) likely provide dynamically important non-thermal pressure support in the circumgalactic medium (CGM), but how their transport physics shapes observable absorption signatures remains uncertain. We investigate whether absorption-line diagnostics can distinguish between different CR transport regimes in CR-pressure-dominated halos. Using high-resolution simulations, we generate synthetic spectra along large ensembles of sightlines and measure column densities, equivalent widths, covering fractions (CFs), velocity widths, abundance ratios, and stacked absorption profiles for ions tracing cool, warm, and hot gas. We find that the effective CR transport speed strongly regulates the multiphase structure of the CGM. Efficient CR transport enhances the formation of cool ($T\sim10^4$ K) and warm ($T\sim10^5$ K) gas, leading to deeper and broader absorption lines of low- and intermediate-ionization species. The two-moment CR transport model produces the strongest MgII and SiII absorption and reaches MgII CFs consistent with the range inferred for star-forming galaxies. In contrast, slow CR transport underproduces cool, low-ionization gas and yields substantially weaker absorption. We also find that the origin of CIV-bearing gas changes with CR transport: slow transport mainly produces extended warm halo gas, whereas efficient transport shifts much of the CIV absorption into mixing layers around cool clouds. The high-ionization tracer OVI responds more weakly, indicating that CR transport primarily regulates the cool condensed phase and its interfaces rather than the volume-filling hot halo. These findings suggest that absorption-line measurements of cool and transition-phase gas can provide valuable constraints on the effective transport of CRs through the CGM.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how cosmic ray (CR) transport physics affects absorption-line diagnostics in the circumgalactic medium (CGM). Using high-resolution simulations with synthetic spectra, the authors find that efficient CR transport enhances cool and warm gas formation, producing stronger MgII and SiII absorption, while slow CR transport underproduces these signatures. The results suggest absorption-line measurements can constrain CR transport regimes in galaxy halos.
AI.motivation: To determine whether absorption-line diagnostics can distinguish between different cosmic ray transport regimes in CR-pressure-dominated halos, given that CRs likely provide dynamically important non-thermal pressure support in the CGM but their transport physics and observable signatures remain uncertain.
AI.method: High-resolution simulations with synthetic spectra generated along large ensembles of sightlines, measuring column densities, equivalent widths, covering fractions, velocity widths, abundance ratios, and stacked absorption profiles for ions tracing cool, warm, and hot gas across different CR transport models.
AI.result: Efficient CR transport enhances cool (10^4 K) and warm (10^5 K) gas formation, producing deeper/broader absorption lines of low- and intermediate-ionization species. The two-moment CR transport model produces the strongest MgII and SiII absorption with MgII covering fractions consistent with star-forming galaxies. Slow CR transport underproduces cool gas and yields weaker absorption. CIV origin shifts from extended warm halo (slow transport) to mixing layers around cool clouds (efficient transport). OVI responds weakly.
AI.conclusion: Absorption-line measurements of cool and transition-phase gas can provide valuable constraints on the effective transport of cosmic rays through the CGM.

title: Joint constraints on gravity and stellar orbital anisotropy in massive galaxies
summary: Strong gravitational lensing combined with stellar dynamics provides a complementary route for testing gravity on kiloparsec scales and probing the internal structure of massive galaxies. However, such studies remain limited by degeneracies among the mass-density profile, stellar orbital anisotropy and external convergence, and by modelling assumptions, especially when only single-aperture velocity dispersions are available. Here we develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework to disentangle gravity and stellar orbital anisotropy from other effects at the population level. By reconstructing the lens mass distribution with a flexible broken power-law model and propagating its posterior uncertainty into the predicted velocity dispersion, we obtain a likelihood for each lens in the plane of stellar orbital anisotropy and an effective mismatch parameter. This parameter encapsulates projection bias, external convergence, cosmological distance ratios and deviations from general relativity via the post-Newtonian parameter $γ_{\rm PPN}$. Applying this framework to 121 galaxy-scale lenses, we find $γ_{\rm PPN}=1.027^{+0.099}_{-0.095}$, consistent with general relativity, and obtain $2σ$ evidence that the stellar orbits of massive galaxies have become more radially biased over the past $\sim6$ Gyr. Forecasts show that future samples of order $10^5$ lenses could enable sub-percent tests of gravity, precise measurements of orbital-structure evolution and complementary constraints on the cosmological matter-density parameter.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian framework combines strong lensing and stellar dynamics to simultaneously constrain gravity (via the post-Newtonian parameter γ_PPN) and stellar orbital anisotropy using 121 galaxy-scale lenses, finding γ_PPN=1.027^{+0.099}_{-0.095} (consistent with GR) and 2σ evidence for increasingly radial stellar orbits over the past ~6 Gyr.
AI.motivation: Strong gravitational lensing combined with stellar dynamics provides a complementary route for testing gravity on kiloparsec scales and probing the internal structure of massive galaxies, but such studies remain limited by degeneracies among mass-density profile, stellar orbital anisotropy and external convergence, and by modelling assumptions.
AI.method: The authors develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework that reconstructs the lens mass distribution with a flexible broken power-law model, propagates posterior uncertainty into predicted velocity dispersion, and obtains a likelihood for each lens in the plane of stellar orbital anisotropy and an effective mismatch parameter (encapsulating projection bias, external convergence, cosmological distance ratios and deviations from GR via γ_PPN).
AI.result: Applied to 121 galaxy-scale lenses, γ_PPN=1.027^{+0.099}_{-0.095} (consistent with GR), and 2σ evidence that stellar orbits of massive galaxies have become more radially biased over the past ~6 Gyr.
AI.conclusion: Future samples of ~10^5 lenses could enable sub-percent tests of gravity, precise measurements of orbital-structure evolution and complementary constraints on the cosmological matter-density parameter.

title: First detection of ultra-fast outflows in a quiescent galaxy
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, and 3 tables, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Outflows in active galactic nuclei (AGN) are recognized as a fundamental mechanism driving the co-evolution of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their host galaxies. Although powerful outflows are frequently detected in gas-rich, active star-forming galaxies, their existence and potential impact within gas-poor, quiescent galaxies remain poorly understood. We report the first detection of a powerful ultra-fast outflow (UFO) in a nearby quiescent galaxy KUG 1208+386, providing a multiscale analysis of AGN winds from nuclear to galactic scales. We detect a nuclear X-ray UFO with a velocity of $v_{out} \approx -0.07c$ and a kinetic power of $\dot{E}_{\rm UFO}=(0.8\mbox{--}6.5) \times 10^{43}$erg/s, sufficient to drive effective AGN feedback ($\dot{E}_{\rm UFO}/L_\mathrm{Edd}=(1\mbox{--}8)\%$) and far exceeding the galactic [OIII] outflow power $\sim 10^{40}$ erg/s. Host galaxy analysis reveals a massive quiescent system (specific star formation rate $\sim3\times10^{-12}\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$) that has been quenched $\sim$9 Gyr ago. The central AGN is obscured by a line-of-sight (LOS) column density of $\log (N_\mathrm{H}^\mathrm{LOS}/\mathrm{cm}^{-2})\sim23$ and the circumnuclear scattering material is Compton-thick $\log(N_\mathrm{H}^\mathrm{scatter}/\mathrm{cm}^{-2})=24.7^{+0.8}_{-0.5}$. The discovery of a nuclear UFO in a long-quenched massive galaxy challenges the paradigm that UFOs are exclusive to gas-rich, star-forming systems, suggesting instead that they are governed by the local circumnuclear environments, rather than the global gas reservoir. Our results indicate that episodic, powerful winds can maintain the quiescent state of KUG 1208+386 over Gyr timescales, supporting a wind-driven `maintenance' mode of AGN feedback that is distinct from the classical jet mode.

AI.tldr: First detection of a powerful ultra-fast outflow (UFO, v ≈ -0.07c) in a long-quenched quiescent galaxy KUG 1208+386, demonstrating that UFOs are not exclusive to gas-rich star-forming systems and can sustain AGN maintenance feedback over Gyr timescales.
AI.motivation: While AGN outflows are well-studied in gas-rich, active star-forming galaxies, their existence and potential impact in gas-poor, quiescent galaxies remain poorly understood, motivating the search for UFOs in such environments.
AI.method: Multiscale analysis combining nuclear X-ray spectroscopy (detecting UFO absorption line at v ≈ -0.07c) with host galaxy properties (SED fitting, stellar population analysis) and ionized gas kinematics ([OIII] outflow measurements).
AI.result: Detected a UFO with kinetic power (0.8–6.5)×10⁴³ erg/s (1–8% L_Edd), far exceeding weak galactic [OIII] outflow (~10⁴⁰ erg/s). The host is a massive quiescent system quenched ~9 Gyr ago (sSFR ~3×10⁻¹² yr⁻¹). AGN is obscured (LOS log N_H ~23) with Compton-thick scattering material (log N_H^scatter = 24.7).
AI.conclusion: UFOs are not exclusive to gas-rich, star-forming systems but are governed by local circumnuclear environments. Episodic powerful winds can maintain quiescence over Gyr, supporting a wind-driven "maintenance" mode of AGN feedback distinct from classical jet mode.

title: The direction of rotation of supermassive black holes is unrelated to the direction of rotation of the host galaxy
summary: We compare the apparent directions of rotation in the plane of the sky of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and their host galaxies. The direction of rotation of the galaxy was inferred from the direction of the spiral arms, while the direction of rotation of the AGN was inferred from spectropolarimetry, where the change in relative polarization position angle (PA) across broad lines is believed to be caused by equatorial scattering. The numbers of co-rotating and counter-rotating AGNs are equal. Studies of the relative position angles of radio jets have implied that there is a "zone of avoidance" where jets avoid being in the plane of disk galaxies. We point out that bi-conical narrow-line-region outflows also avoid the plane of the host galaxy. The equal numbers of co-rotating and counter-rotating AGNs exclude the hypothesis that the "zone of avoidance" is due to a lack of large tilts of the black hole rotating axis relative to the host galaxy rotation axis. Our results imply that the relative orientations of spin axes are random, at least for the black hole mass range we consider. We propose that changes in the broad-line polarization PA with wavelength that do not closely follow the predictions of the simple equatorial scattering model are a consequence of the scattering dust being clumpy. We note a couple of cases of possible changes in PA over several years, which, if real, could be due to motions of the dust clumps or changing anisotropy of the continuum emission.

AI.tldr: This study compares the rotation directions of AGNs and their host galaxies using spectropolarimetry and spiral arm morphology. Equal numbers of co-rotating and counter-rotating AGNs are found, ruling out hypotheses about jet "zone of avoidance" being due to aligned spin axes. The results suggest random spin-axis orientations relative to host galaxies.
AI.motivation: To investigate the relative alignment between AGN rotation axes (inferred from spectropolarimetry) and host galaxy rotation axes (inferred from spiral arm direction), and to test hypotheses about the "zone of avoidance" where jets avoid the galactic plane.
AI.method: Compared AGN rotation direction (from broad-line polarization position angle changes via equatorial scattering) with host galaxy rotation direction (from spiral arm morphology). Analyzed co-rotation vs. counter-rotation statistics and examined radio jet and NLR outflow orientation relative to galaxy plane.
AI.result: Equal numbers of co-rotating and counter-rotating AGNs were found. This excludes the hypothesis that the jet "zone of avoidance" is caused by a lack of large tilts between black hole spin axis and galaxy rotation axis. Both jets and bi-conical NLR outflows avoid the plane of the host galaxy.
AI.conclusion: Relative orientations of AGN spin axes and host galaxy rotation axes appear to be random (for the black hole mass range studied). Deviations from simple equatorial scattering predictions may be due to clumpy dust. Possible PA changes over years could reflect dust clump motions or varying continuum anisotropy.

title: XRISM Reveals a Kinematically Coherent Core System of the Nearby Cool-Core Cluster Abell 2199
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables, Submitted to PASJ
summary: We present the results of a deep 251 ks XRISM/Resolve observation of the cool core of the galaxy cluster Abell 2199. From the integrated spectrum of the central $3' \times 3'$ Resolve field of view ($104 \times 104 \mathrm{~kpc}^2$), we find that the intracluster medium (ICM) redshift is consistent with that of the brightest cluster galaxy, within the optical-redshift uncertainty. This indicates that they form a kinematically coherent core system, which offset from the mean cluster redshift by $\sim200~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$. The observed velocity dispersion of $\sim100~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$ corresponds to a three-dimensional Mach number of $M_{\mathrm{3D}}=0.16$ and a non-thermal pressure fraction of $P_{\mathrm{NT}}/P_{\mathrm{tot}}=1.4\pm0.2$%. Abell 2199 is one of the most dynamically quiescent relaxed clusters observed with XRISM, despite the presence of radio jets and a plume-like structure possibly associated with sloshing motions. Order-of-magnitude estimates suggest that turbulent dissipation could offset a non-negligible fraction of the radiative cooling losses, with $Q_{\mathrm{turb}}/Q_{\mathrm{cool}}\approx0.2$ for a large-scale driver such as sloshing and larger values for smaller AGN-feedback scales. Finally, we detect a localized enhancement of the Fe XXV He$α$ $y$ line in the southeast region, which spatially coincides with a Chandra surface brightness discontinuity.

AI.tldr: XRISM/Resolve observation of Abell 2199's cool core reveals coherent kinematics with the BCG, low turbulence (M₃D=0.16), non-thermal pressure fraction ~1.4%, potential turbulent dissipation offsetting ~20% of cooling losses, and a localized Fe XXV Heα y line enhancement correlated with a surface brightness discontinuity.
AI.motivation: To characterize the dynamical state and thermodynamic properties of the intracluster medium in the cool core of Abell 2199 using high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy, and to assess the roles of turbulence, AGN feedback, and sloshing in balancing radiative cooling.
AI.method: Deep 251 ks XRISM/Resolve spectroscopic observation of the central 3'×3' (104×104 kpc²) field; line broadening and shift analysis of ICM emission; comparison with optical redshifts; Mach number and non-thermal pressure fraction derivation from velocity dispersion; spatial mapping of Fe XXV Heα line complex.
AI.result: ICM redshift matches BCG within optical uncertainty; velocity dispersion ~100 km/s yields M₃D=0.16 and P_NT/P_tot=1.4±0.2%; turbulent dissipation Q_turb/Q_cool≈0.2 for sloshing-scale drivers; detection of localized Fe XXV Heα y line enhancement coincident with a Chandra surface brightness edge in the southeast region.
AI.conclusion: Abell 2199 is one of the most dynamically quiescent relaxed clusters observed by XRISM; turbulent heating can offset a non-negligible fraction of cooling; the Fe XXV enhancement points to multiphase ICM or non-thermal processes associated with a dynamical perturbation.

title: The dynamical origin of the magnetic field distributions in compressible turbulence
comment: A&A submitted, last stages of referee process
summary: Magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations of isothermal compressible turbulence report that the density distribution is well described by a lognormal with a variance proportional to the flow's Mach number. The distribution of magnetic field strength also has a lognormal component, but includes long, power-law-like tails. In this work, we use semi-analytical arguments to predict the distributions of density and magnetic field strength in compressible turbulent flows. Specifically, in the Lagrangian description of the continuity and the induction equations, we model the velocity gradients of the turbulent flow as a simple random process, essentially turning these equations into stochastic differential equations. Integrating them leads to a lognormal distribution for the density field and the strength of the magnetic field. The power-law tails in the magnetic field PDF appear when we introduce intermittent shocks due to sampling rare events. Gradually increasing the frequency of these events, essentially going closer to a continuous process, leads to lognormal-like distributions again. The asymmetry is connected to the relative abundance of slow and fast shocks. An overabundance of fast MHD shocks produces a high-value tail, while the contrary produces low-value tails. We propose that the appearance of power-law tails along lognormals in turbulent flows is the signature of the co-existence of continuous, diffusion-like propagation combined with localized, intermittent events.

AI.tldr: The paper uses semi-analytical stochastic differential equations to model density and magnetic field distributions in MHD turbulence, showing lognormal distributions arise from continuous diffusion-like processes while power-law tails emerge from intermittent shock events, with tail asymmetry linked to the relative abundance of slow versus fast MHD shocks.
AI.motivation: To understand and predict the statistical distributions of density and magnetic field strength in compressible MHD turbulent flows, specifically explaining why density follows a lognormal while magnetic field strength exhibits power-law tails alongside a lognormal component.
AI.method: The authors employ semi-analytical arguments by treating the continuity and induction equations as stochastic differential equations in a Lagrangian framework, modeling velocity gradients as random processes. They introduce intermittent shocks as rare events to explain power-law tails and vary shock frequency to study transition back to lognormal distributions.
AI.result: 1) Both density and magnetic field strength follow lognormal distributions under continuous diffusion-like propagation. 2) Power-law tails in the magnetic field PDF arise from intermittent shock events. 3) High-value tails correspond to fast MHD shock overabundance; low-value tails correspond to slow MHD shock overabundance. 4) Increasing shock frequency toward a continuous process restores lognormal-like behavior.
AI.conclusion: The coexistence of power-law tails and lognormal distributions in turbulent MHD flows is the signature of combined continuous diffusion-like propagation and localized intermittent events (shocks).

title: Fast Dynamical Modelling of Milky Way Globular Clusters -- I. Implications for Initial Cluster Densities
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to ApJ, comments welcome
summary: We infer the initial conditions of Milky Way (MW) globular clusters (GCs) from present-day observations, through the coupling of recently updated rapid cluster evolution models with multimass equilibrium models. This novel method is validated by fitting to simulated observations of a large grid of star-by-star Monte Carlo models, demonstrating that we are able to recover cluster properties like the total mass, half-mass radius/density and black hole (BH) mass fraction, both initially and at the present day, across a large region of parameter space. We apply this framework to a sample of 40 MW GCs, fitting to a suite of observed radial profiles of number densities, proper motions, line-of-sight velocities and stellar mass functions. From these fits we infer a distribution of initial half-mass densities with a median and $1σ$ width, across our sample, of $ρ_{h,0} = 10^{6.4\pm0.9}\,{M_\odot pc^{-3}}$, higher than what is found for young massive clusters in the Local Universe and in line with young clusters at high redshift. We also find stellar initial mass functions that are bottom-light in comparison to canonical prescriptions, and relatively small present-day BH mass fractions ($\lesssim 1.5\%$). We discuss the implications of these initial cluster densities for observations of high-redshift proto-GCs, binary BH merger rates and intermediate-mass BHs (IMBHs) in GCs. Finally, we quantify how these densities may depend on assumptions typically made surrounding BH formation and natal kicks.

AI.tldr: This paper infers the initial conditions of Milky Way globular clusters by coupling rapid cluster evolution models with multimass equilibrium models, fitting to present-day observations to recover initial cluster properties, and finds high initial half-mass densities, bottom-light IMFs, and low present-day BH mass fractions.
AI.motivation: To infer the initial conditions (total mass, half-mass radius/density, BH mass fraction) of Milky Way globular clusters from present-day observations, using a novel method that couples rapid cluster evolution models with multimass equilibrium models.
AI.method: Coupling of recently updated rapid cluster evolution models with multimass equilibrium models; validated by fitting to simulated observations of a large grid of star-by-star Monte Carlo models; applied to a sample of 40 MW GCs fitting to observed radial profiles of number densities, proper motions, line-of-sight velocities, and stellar mass functions.
AI.result: Inferred initial half-mass densities with median $ρ_{h,0} = 10^{6.4±0.9}\,M_\odot pc^{-3}$, higher than young massive clusters in the Local Universe and in line with high-redshift young clusters; stellar IMFs that are bottom-light; present-day BH mass fractions $\lesssim 1.5\%$.
AI.conclusion: The inferred high initial densities have implications for observations of high-redshift proto-GCs, binary BH merger rates, and IMBHs in GCs; results depend on assumptions about BH formation and natal kicks.

title: Reconnection diagnostics for vortex tangles in Bose-condensed and superfluid dark matter halos
summary: Bose-Einstein-condensed (BEC) and superfluid dark-matter (SFDM) halos can contain coherent, wave-supported cores whose angular momentum is carried by quantized vortices. When vortices form a tangle, reconnections convert part of the vortex kinetic energy into dark phonons, density waves, Kelvin waves, and vortex loops, providing a microscopic channel by which SFDM vortex structure can affect halo-core evolution. We estimate the dynamical importance of this channel by combining the local Gross-Pitaevskii reconnection law with a halo-scale vortex-line density calibrated against Schrödinger-Poisson simulations. In the minimal model the released energy stays in the dark sector, and standard-model luminosity requires additional portal physics.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how quantized vortex reconnections in Bose-Einstein condensed/superfluid dark matter halos can convert vortex kinetic energy into dark phonons and other excitations, potentially affecting halo-core evolution, and estimates the dynamical significance of this process using a combined Gross-Pitaevskii and Schrödinger-Poisson approach.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of quantized vortices and their reconnections in the evolution of BEC/SFDM halo cores, specifically how vortex kinetic energy dissipation via reconnection provides a microscopic channel affecting halo-core dynamics.
AI.method: Combines the local Gross-Pitaevskii reconnection law with halo-scale vortex-line density calibrated against Schrödinger-Poisson simulations to estimate the dynamical importance of vortex reconnection energy release.
AI.result: In the minimal model, the energy released from vortex reconnections stays within the dark sector, and generating standard-model luminous signals requires additional portal physics.
AI.conclusion: Vortex reconnection provides a viable microscopic channel for energy transfer in SFDM halos, but visible electromagnetic signatures are not naturally produced without introducing beyond-minimal model couplings to the standard model.

title: The MAGPI Survey: Evidence for Non-Universal Resolved Dust Attenuation Relations Beyond the Local Universe
summary: We study the spatially resolved relation between dust attenuation ($A_V$) and star formation rate surface density ($Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$) in galaxies from the MAGPI survey ($0.25 < z < 0.42$). Using Balmer-decrement-based attenuation maps for 178 galaxies, we investigate whether the locally calibrated resolved $A_V$--$Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ relation remains valid at intermediate redshift by comparing MAGPI with the local relation measured from MaNGA. We find a clear positive correlation between $A_V$ and $Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ in MAGPI, with systematically higher attenuation than in MaNGA at fixed $Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$. After matching galaxies in stellar mass ($M_{*}$) and offset from the star-forming main sequence ($Δ$SFMS), MAGPI galaxies remain more attenuated than MaNGA galaxies at fixed $Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$. The attenuation excess is strongest for galaxies below the SFMS ($ΔA_V \sim 0.40$ mag), weaker for galaxies on the SFMS ($ΔA_V \sim 0.28$ mag), and minimal for galaxies above the SFMS ($ΔA_V \sim 0.07$ mag). The dependence of the offset on $Δ$SFMS suggests that nebular attenuation on kpc scales is regulated not only by local star formation activity, but also by the global evolutionary state of the host galaxy. Together, these results indicate that the resolved $A_V$--$Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ relation is not universal, and that locally calibrated attenuation relations may not fully describe galaxies at intermediate redshift. This highlights the need for attenuation calibrations that account for galaxy population and redshift when interpreting spatially resolved galaxy properties.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the resolved dust attenuation (A_V) versus star formation rate surface density (Σ_SFR) relation in 178 MAGPI survey galaxies at intermediate redshift (0.25<z<0.42). Compared to local MaNGA galaxies, MAGPI galaxies show systematically higher attenuation at fixed Σ_SFR, even after matching in stellar mass and star-forming main sequence offset (ΔSFMS). The excess attenuation depends on ΔSFMS: strongest below the SFMS (~0.40 mag), weaker on the SFMS (~0.28 mag), and minimal above it (~0.07 mag). This suggests the resolved A_V-Σ_SFR relation is not universal and local calibrations may not apply at higher redshift.
AI.motivation: To test whether the locally calibrated resolved A_V-Σ_SFR relation (from MaNGA) remains valid at intermediate redshift (z~0.3), and to understand how global evolutionary state influences kpc-scale dust attenuation.
AI.method: Balmer-decrement-based attenuation maps for 178 MAGPI galaxies (0.25<z<0.42) are constructed. The resolved A_V-Σ_SFR relation is measured and directly compared with the local relation from MaNGA, with controls on stellar mass and ΔSFMS to isolate redshift and evolutionary-state effects.
AI.result: MAGPI galaxies show systematically higher A_V than MaNGA at fixed Σ_SFR. After matching in M* and ΔSFMS, the excess persists: ΔA_V~0.40 mag below SFMS, ~0.28 mag on SFMS, ~0.07 mag above SFMS.
AI.conclusion: The resolved A_V-Σ_SFR relation is not universal; local calibrations may not fully describe intermediate-redshift galaxies. Attenuation models must account for both redshift and evolutionary state.

title: GalPort: Investigation of the bar in action-angle space
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 1 table, Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Computing
summary: GalPort is a Python package for analysing the orbital dynamics of evolving disc galaxy numerical models in action-angle space. The package implements novel numerical methods for efficiently estimating actions, angles, and frequencies across different, particle-specific timescales: on the scale of radial or vertical oscillation and on the resonant libration/circulation timescale. The algorithm allows calculation of these dynamic quantities simultaneously at all time steps of the simulated galactic evolution. With this tool, one can trace orbital behaviour within time-varying galactic potentials and classify orbits (resonantly trapped, circulating, or passing through a resonance) based on their angle evolution. GalPort also includes specialised options for analysing the phase-space structure of a galactic bar in the disc plane and along its major axis. We demonstrate the package's performance on a typical N-body model of a barred galaxy, obtaining the global distributions of actions and frequencies and performing a detailed orbital decomposition. The code is publicly available under the MIT license at: https://github.com/vdzozulia/galport

AI.tldr: GalPort is a Python package for analyzing orbital dynamics of disc galaxy models in action-angle space, with novel numerical methods for efficient calculation across different timescales and orbit classification.
AI.motivation: To provide a tool for tracing orbital behavior in time-varying galactic potentials and classifying orbits (resonantly trapped, circulating, or passing through resonance) based on angle evolution, addressing the need for analyzing evolving disc galaxy simulations.
AI.method: Implements novel numerical methods to estimate actions, angles, and frequencies across particle-specific timescales (radial/vertical oscillation and resonant libration/circulation), calculating these simultaneously at all time steps. Includes specialized options for analyzing galactic bar phase-space structure.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a typical N-body barred galaxy model, obtaining global distributions of actions and frequencies and performing detailed orbital decomposition.
AI.conclusion: GalPort enables comprehensive orbital analysis in evolving disc galaxies, is publicly available under MIT license, and supports orbit classification based on angle evolution.

title: Quantifying Environmental Effects on Galaxy Properties using Non-spherical Voids Identified from SDSS DR7
summary: Cosmic voids provide a distinct low-density region for studying the environmental effects of galaxy properties. Using the SDSS DR7 catalog, we identify non-spherical voids via Voronoi tessellation and the watershed algorithm, and classify void galaxies based on their local volume. We compare and find that void galaxies classified by this method are systematically less massive, fainter, bluer, and have higher specific star formation rate (sSFR) than non-void galaxies and all galaxy samples. We then divide void and non-void galaxies into stellar mass bins to focus on the environmental dependence of $g-r$ color and sSFR. By further classifying galaxies into blue/red and star-forming/quiescent populations, we calculate the ratio of blue to red and star-forming to quiescent for void and non-void galaxies separately. Comparing the ratio of the void value to the non-void value for both metrics presents an overall decreasing trend with stellar mass $M_*$ over the $9.4-10.4$ range in $\log[M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot]$, indicating a stronger environmental effect in lower-mass systems. These results show that our classification of void galaxies in non-spherical voids based on local volume offers a robust approach for quantifying the influence of underdense environments on galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: Using SDSS DR7 data and watershed void identification, the authors classify void galaxies by local volume and find they are less massive, fainter, bluer, and have higher sSFR than non-void galaxies. The ratio of blue/red and star-forming/quiescent populations between void and non-void decreases with stellar mass, indicating stronger environmental effects in lower-mass systems.
AI.motivation: To study how low-density cosmic void environments influence galaxy properties, particularly color and star formation activity, and to test whether non-spherical void definition based on local volume yields robust environmental classifications.
AI.method: Non-spherical voids identified from SDSS DR7 using Voronoi tessellation and watershed algorithm; void galaxies classified by local volume density. Galaxies split into stellar mass bins; blue/red and star-forming/quiescent classifications used to compute population ratios between void and non-void samples.
AI.result: Void galaxies are systematically less massive, fainter, bluer, and have higher sSFR. The void-to-non-void ratio of blue/red and star-forming/quiescent populations decreases with stellar mass over log(M*/M⊙) = 9.4–10.4, showing stronger environmental effects in lower-mass systems.
AI.conclusion: Classifying void galaxies by local volume in non-spherical voids provides a robust method for quantifying the influence of underdense environments on galaxy evolution.

title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Searching for radio-selected \Euclid-dark galaxies in the EDF-N
comment: Paper accepted by A&A, 20 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables
summary: We present and investigate the properties of a sample of radio-selected, Euclid-dark galaxies, identified from LOFAR HBA observations at 144 MHz within the Euclid Deep Field-North (EDF-N). Starting from radio sources lacking optical counterparts in previous surveys, but detected with Spitzer/IRAC, we identified 166 galaxies with no emission at a more than $3σ$ level in Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1) images, and no matches in the Euclid Q1 catalogue. To minimise contamination from nearby sources, we selected a sub-sample of 88 isolated galaxies. By exploiting multi-band images and catalogues available for the EDF-N, we inferred the physical properties of our sample via SED fitting. The resulting redshift distribution spans $0.4 \leq z_\mathrm{ph} \leq 5.0$. We used recent sub-arcsecond imaging from the International LOFAR Telescope to constrain the nature of the compact radio emission through brightness temperature estimates. By combining this information with the radio excess relative to the infrared/radio correlation (IRRC), we searched for possible active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity. Approximately 40% of our sources show evidence of AGN activity. The Euclid-dark sources detected in the far-infrared are consistent with a population of heavily obscured, massive star-forming galaxies with high star formation rates. Their location above the star-forming main sequence is consistent with similar near-infrared-dark galaxy populations reported in the literature. We also performed a UV-to-radio median stacking analysis, finding that the two subsamples exhibit similar global physical properties and differ primarily in their radio emission. These preliminary results indicate that the wide area covered by Euclid enables the identification of a higher fraction of systems in which intense star formation and AGN activity coexist, likely capturing a key phase of galaxy--black hole co-evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and studies 166 Euclid-dark galaxies (with 88 isolated) from LOFAR radio observations in the Euclid Deep Field-North, finding they are massive, obscured star-forming galaxies at z~0.4-5.0, ~40% show AGN activity, and they lie above the star-forming main sequence, representing a key phase of galaxy-black hole co-evolution.
AI.motivation: To characterize Euclid-dark galaxies — radio-selected sources with no optical counterparts in Euclid Q1 data — and understand their physical properties, obscuration, and AGN activity, leveraging Euclid's wide area to capture rare co-evolution phases.
AI.method: Selected 166 radio sources (144 MHz LOFAR HBA) with no Euclid Q1 optical emission (>3σ) but detected in Spitzer/IRAC; isolated a sub-sample of 88 galaxies free from nearby contamination; performed SED fitting using multi-band data; used sub-arcsecond International LOFAR Telescope imaging for brightness temperature estimates; combined with IRRC to identify AGN; conducted UV-to-radio median stacking analysis.
AI.result: Redshift range 0.4 ≤ z_ph ≤ 5.0; ~40% show AGN activity; Euclid-dark FIR-detected sources are heavily obscured, massive star-forming galaxies with high SFRs above the main sequence; two subsamples (isolated and full) share similar global properties, differing mainly in radio emission.
AI.conclusion: Euclid's wide-area coverage enables identification of a higher fraction of systems where intense star formation and AGN coexist, likely capturing a key phase of galaxy-black hole co-evolution.

title: Beyond traditional emission-line diagnostics: using autoencoders to uncover active galactic nuclei in DESI spectra
summary: The growing volume of spectroscopic data in modern surveys motivates data-driven approaches that complement traditional emission-line diagnostics for active galactic nuclei (AGN) identification. We present a machine learning framework that exploits the full optical spectrum using unsupervised representation learning within a semi-supervised classification scheme. We use the SPENDER autoencoder to compress DESI galaxy spectra into a low-dimensional latent space and classify sources through a k-d tree nearest-neighbor search. The model is trained on 50,222 DESI Main Survey spectra from the Guadalupe dataset and released as part of Data Release 1 (DR1), restricted to z <= 0.5. We validate the performance using labels derived from FastSpecFit's emission line measurements defining seven galaxy classes: AGN, broad-line (BL), composite, star-forming, passive, retired, and Other. The method achieves high accuracies for AGN (0.952) and broad-line AGN (0.965), reliably identifying these sources even in low signal-to-noise spectra and recovering AGN missed by standard single-diagnostic methods. Our classification metrics are benchmarked against traditional diagnostics, and we show they represent lower limits of the model's true performance. We also find that the learned latent space correlates with key galaxy properties such as stellar mass and star-formation rate, demonstrating that it captures physically meaningful information. These results show that unsupervised spectral representation learning, implemented within a semi-supervised classification framework, provides a scalable and effective approach for constructing more complete AGN catalogues for current and future spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a semi-supervised machine learning framework using a SPENDER autoencoder to compress DESI galaxy spectra into a latent space, then classifies galaxies (including AGN, broad-line AGN, star-forming, etc.) via k-d tree nearest-neighbor search. It achieves high accuracy (AGN: 0.952, broad-line: 0.965) and recovers AGN missed by traditional diagnostics, while the latent space correlates with physically meaningful galaxy properties like stellar mass and star-formation rate.
AI.motivation: The growing volume of spectroscopic data in modern surveys necessitates data-driven approaches that go beyond traditional emission-line diagnostics for AGN identification, motivating a scalable, unsupervised representation learning method.
AI.method: The method uses the SPENDER autoencoder to compress full optical DESI spectra into a low-dimensional latent space, followed by a k-d tree nearest-neighbor search for semi-supervised classification. Training is on 50,222 DESI Main Survey spectra (z ≤ 0.5) from the Guadalupe dataset (DR1). Seven galaxy classes are defined using FastSpecFit emission-line measurements.
AI.result: The method achieves accuracies of 0.952 for AGN and 0.965 for broad-line AGN, reliably identifies AGN in low signal-to-noise spectra, recovers AGN missed by single-diagnostic methods, and the latent space correlates with stellar mass and star-formation rate.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised spectral representation learning within a semi-supervised classification framework is a scalable and effective approach for constructing more complete AGN catalogues for current and future spectroscopic surveys.

title: A machine learning approach to estimating HI deficiency in galaxies
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures. This is the author manuscript prior to peer review; the final published version is available in PASP
summary: Measurements of the HI content of galaxies serve as an important tracer for probing the impact of environment on galaxy evolution. More specifically, the HI deficiency (defined as the difference between expected unaltered and observed HI content of a galaxy) is closely related with environmental effects, which are most significant in large groups and clusters. In this work, we aim to estimate the HI deficiency of ALFALFA galaxies and investigate its relation with galactic environment. Using a random forest machine learning algorithm, we developed a predictive model capable of estimating the original HI content of a galaxy based solely on its optical properties. The model was trained on a subsample of 6 982 isolated ALFALFA galaxies with optical photometric data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Our predictive model outperforms the traditional approach, in which HI mass is linearly related to optical size (both on a logarithmic scale). The model achieves RMSE $\approx$ 0.22 dex and $R^2 \approx$ 0.80, compared with RMSE $\approx$ 0.26 dex and $R^2 \approx$ 0.70 for the traditional method. We applied this model to predict the expected HI content for non-isolated ALFALFA galaxies, enabling the calculation of HI deficiency. Controlling for the effects of internal factors, like stellar mass and presence of AGN, we find an increase in binned median HI deficiency of 0.15 dex attributable to environmental effects. In addition, we evaluate the temporal evolution of the predicted HI mass, and associated HI deficiency, due to the evolving stellar populations, following a gas removal event.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a random forest model trained on isolated ALFALFA galaxies to predict HI content from optical properties, computes HI deficiency for non-isolated galaxies, and finds environmental effects cause ~0.15 dex increase in median HI deficiency.
AI.motivation: HI content measurements trace environmental impacts on galaxy evolution; HI deficiency is linked to environmental effects in groups and clusters.
AI.method: A random forest machine learning model was trained on 6,982 isolated ALFALFA galaxies with SDSS optical data to predict HI content from optical properties alone, outperforming the traditional log-linear HI mass vs. optical size relationship.
AI.result: The model achieves RMSE ≈ 0.22 dex and R² ≈ 0.80 (vs. 0.26 dex and 0.70 for the traditional method). Environmental effects cause a binned median HI deficiency increase of 0.15 dex.
AI.conclusion: The random forest model reliably predicts expected HI content, enabling robust HI deficiency measurements that reveal environmental quenching effects, and can track temporal evolution of HI mass following gas removal.

title: Milky Way Atlas: A radial-velocity-resolved, three-dimensional map of H I within 1.25 kpc
comment: 24 pages, 21 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present a velocity-resolved three-dimensional map of local atomic hydrogen (HI) within 1.25 kpc of the Sun, tackling the challenge of converting emission from position-position-velocity space into true 3D structure. Our method combines the HI4PI full-sky survey with the Edenhofer et al. (2024) 3D dust map in the framework of Information Field Theory, enabling a joint reconstruction of the local HI density, radial velocity field, and effective line width while also separating emission arising inside the mapped local volume from more distant Galactic HI. The inference is driven by morphological matching between dust and HI structures together with kinematic coherence in 3D space. Synthetic data tests show that the method recovers the local density and velocity structure, even in the presence of substantial contamination from distant emission. The resulting map reveals a smoother, more diffuse local HI distribution than the dust, a declining HI-to-dust ratio toward high dust column densities consistent with the atomic-to-molecular transition, and a velocity field that captures both large-scale Galactic rotation and local non-circular velocities. Independent comparisons with maser and young stellar cluster velocities agree with the recovered kinematics. This HI map provides a new three-dimensional, kinematically resolved view of the nearby atomic interstellar medium and a foundation for localising other velocity-resolved Galactic emission in physical space.

AI.tldr: A velocity-resolved 3D map of local atomic hydrogen (HI) within 1.25 kpc of the Sun is reconstructed by combining HI4PI survey data with a 3D dust map using Information Field Theory, revealing the local HI density, velocity field, and line width while separating nearby from distant emission.
AI.motivation: To convert HI emission from position-position-velocity space into true 3D structure, overcoming the challenge of disentangling local from distant Galactic HI, in order to obtain a kinematically resolved view of the nearby atomic interstellar medium.
AI.method: Combines the HI4PI full-sky survey with the Edenhofer et al. (2024) 3D dust map within the framework of Information Field Theory, jointly reconstructing local HI density, radial velocity field, and effective line width while separating local emission from distant Galactic HI contamination.
AI.result: The map reveals a smoother, more diffuse local HI distribution than dust, a declining HI-to-dust ratio at high dust column densities (consistent with the atomic-to-molecular transition), and a velocity field capturing both large-scale Galactic rotation and local non-circular motions, validated against maser and young stellar cluster velocities.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a new three-dimensional, kinematically resolved view of the nearby atomic ISM and establishes a foundation for localising other velocity-resolved Galactic emission in physical space.

title: Tracing the Evolution of the Balmer Break from Cosmic Dawn to Cosmic Noon with JWST
comment: 22 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: The Balmer break (BB) is a key spectral feature for constraining stellar population ages, star formation histories, and redshifts of high-redshift sources. The redshift evolution and distribution of BB strength, together with the properties of BB galaxies, constrain stellar population characteristics and the nature of star formation across cosmic epochs. However, a systematic and unbiased characterization of BB strengths across the full galaxy population remains limited with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We aim to characterize the redshift evolution of BB strength over $z=3.5$-10 and its distribution across different epochs using photometry. We also examine correlations between BB strength and key physical parameters within these redshift intervals. We further assess the implications of BB galaxies for the nature of star formation and stellar populations at $z>3.5$. We used the JWST NIRCam photometric observations taken as part of various programs, including CEERS, JADES, FRESCO, and PRIMER. We estimated the BB strength of the objects with two adjacent broadband filters in various redshift windows between redshifts 3 and 10, which exclude strong line contamination. We employ the SED-fitting code CIGALE for both SED fitting and the generation of mock galaxy simulations. We find that the median Balmer break strength (expressed as a flux ratio) increases from cosmic dawn to cosmic noon, from 1.1 to 1.5, primarily driven by the age of the stellar population. These estimations are in agreement with the latest spectroscopic estimations in the literature. We identify objects with extremely large BB strengths (BB$>3.0$) at $z=3.5$-4 and $z=7$-10, indicating strong extinction combined with an old stellar population and the presence of Little Red Dots (LRDs) in the former, and predominantly LRDs in the latter.[abridged]

AI.tldr: This study uses JWST NIRCam photometry (CEERS, JADES, FRESCO, PRIMER) to characterize the redshift evolution of Balmer break (BB) strength over z=3.5-10. The median BB strength increases from 1.1 at cosmic dawn to 1.5 at cosmic noon, driven by stellar population age. Extremely large BB (>3.0) objects at z=3.5-4 and z=7-10 indicate strong extinction, old stellar populations, and Little Red Dots (LRDs).
AI.motivation: A systematic and unbiased characterization of Balmer break strengths across the full galaxy population at high redshift (z>3.5) remains limited with JWST, despite BB being a key spectral feature for constraining stellar populations, star formation histories, and redshifts.
AI.method: JWST NIRCam photometric observations from CEERS, JADES, FRESCO, and PRIMER programs were used. BB strength was estimated using two adjacent broadband filters in various redshift windows (z=3-10) excluding strong line contamination. SED fitting employed CIGALE for both fitting and mock galaxy simulations.
AI.result: Median BB strength increases from 1.1 (cosmic dawn) to 1.5 (cosmic noon), driven by stellar population age. Objects with extremely large BB (>3.0) found at z=3.5-4 and z=7-10, attributed to strong extinction + old stellar populations (z=3.5-4) and predominantly LRDs (z=7-10). Results agree with latest spectroscopic estimations.
AI.conclusion: The Balmer break evolves significantly from cosmic dawn to cosmic noon, primarily driven by stellar age. Extreme BB objects are linked to Little Red Dots and highly extincted old stellar populations, providing constraints on star formation nature and stellar populations at z>3.5.
